en: The Saddabindu Treatise.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
To him by whom not even an atom of [untruth] was taught among the doctrines to be known.
Having paid homage to that Saṅgha of the True Dhamma, I shall begin this *Saddabindu* (Drop of Phonetics).
The nine numbers beginning with *ka* are, in order: *ṇa*, *ta*, *di*, *yā*, and so forth;
the five numbers for the feet are reckoned as *suñña*, *nāma*, *sara*, and *añña*.

In the past, there were [the words] *sare*, *heva*, *sarā*, *pubbe*, with elision (*lutta*) and augmentation (*āgama*), as well as lengthening and shortening of vowels (*dīgha-rassa-ādi-sambhava*); [the words] *byañjana*, *ācāga*, *māvā*, and *vī*.
Kāka, Āsena, Agato, and Isi, by means of which he demonstrated his supernormal power (*iddhi*) to Maccu.
For those who are without kings, village chiefs, or messengers, women were made to perform the task of listening.
Thus ends the section on the *saṇḍhikappa*.
[The following are] the Buddha, the male, the youth, the sage, the king, the brahmin, and the friend.
Yata and other embodied beings, the Teacher, Father, Abhibhū,
and Vidū; Kaññā, Mmāra, Attithipa, Kkharaṇī, Nadiruma, Tātabhū,
Napuṃsaka, Itiya, Anta, and Padakamma-dadhāyuṇo.
By including what has already been mentioned here, [the forms] *suddho*, *asya*, and so forth occur in the masculine (*kāpuṃse*);
*vimalā* occurs with those ending in *-jā*; *thyaṃ* and *pañca* occur with those ending in *-dā* and *-dhika*;
and in the neuter (*napuṃsake*), from the usage of *janaka*, they occur ending in *-ti*.
All nouns, compounds, and secondary derivatives (taddhita) follow the rules of effort (padhāna);
likewise, genders, particles, and so forth, as well as suffixes such as *tato*, *lu*, *tta*, *avas*, and *ādi*,
are established according to the grammatical rules (*sutta*), including those beginning with *vatta* and *amanādi*.
Thus the section on Names is completed.
In the case of *cha*, *kāra*, *kesa*, *sāmī*, *samāsa*, *hoti*, *sambhava*, *taddhita*, *akartṛ*, *kamma*,
*sa*, *pada*, *okāsa*, and *sāmī*, [the following rules apply].
The three grammatical cases (sādhattaya) are explained as being used for the agent (kitaka) and the instrument (sādhana);
when the first case is stated, it applies everywhere, and when not stated, the second case and others are understood.
This was spoken by the Sage with his mind, and praised by the Buddha in the forest.
One who has entered the cycle of existence practices meditation for the sake of its cessation;
thus ends the section on grammatical agents.
[The following concerns] compounds (rāsi), dvipadika, and dvanda, according to gender and number.
Bahubbīhi compounds have meanings such as "equal to," "like," or "having a common substratum";
tappurisa compounds include those ending in "acakhema" and "arā"; and kammadhāraya compounds include those ending in "dayā" and "aca.
Furthermore, digu compounds, avyayībhāva compounds, and āhāra compounds—all of these are included here.
Thus ends the section on compound formations (*samāsakappa*).

From this point onward, even according to the *Kaccāyana* system, all secondary suffixes (*taddhita-paccaya*) apply to a single word regardless of any restrictive rule, provided that the meanings are not already expressed by other words.
Thus ends the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).

[The suffixes] *ka*, *tarin*, *nā*, *ññathā*, *akamme*, *tathābhāve*, *tum*, and *eraya* are all included in the root *pac* (to cook) by way of abbreviation; they consist of non-verbal elements (*arūpa*).
Having attained the qualities of a speaker, and having become proficient in other elements through endless applications by means of substitutes, suffixes,
and so forth— thus ends the section on verbs.
All [words] beginning with *kitā* and so forth arise from a single root according to their respective forms, provided there is a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Thus ends the section on *kitaka*.
By this small token, one may know [the extent] in the Victor’s Dispensation,
just as the ocean’s flavor can be known by a single drop;
likewise, the delightful city known as the Piṭaka is for swift entry.
Having purified the path, the non-path, and the state of being on the path within the wilderness of words,
by that very light the jewel-treasure of the *Kaccāyana-ṭīkā* shines like a lamp lit in a corner of the inner chamber.
Thus the treatise *Saddabindu* is completed,
brought to its conclusion by the venerable teacher Dhammādirāja, who, though a youth,
was guided by the ocean-like Dhamma which is both revered and humble.
He who has self-restraint as his wealth and virtue as his ornament, who is like my own eye,
taught me the Dhamma from the Sugata’s scriptures;
he is the beloved one, a mass of merit for the world, and as delightful as a lotus.
Homage to the Great One, the Best of Ascetics, my Teacher!
While dwelling with the wealth of faith, I have understood the flowers called the "Ways of the Noble Ones" (Ariyavaṃsa) by the name of the "Banner."
This was composed by me, Santena, also known as Ñāṇatilaka,
for the benefit of the ignorant.
